title: Why Raft waits for a majority before committing
thesis: Raft log replication is not finished when a request reaches one server. The Leader appends an ordered entry, followers persist it, and only a majority acknowledgement makes it safe to commit and apply.
objectives: Trace a client write through the Leader and followers.
Distinguish “stored on one replica” from “committed history”.
Map majority acknowledgement to the replication code.

terms.plain: The node that accepts writes and chooses the order of log entries.
terms.example: A client sends a write to the Leader, which appends the new entry.

terms.plain: A node that copies entries from the Leader and can vote in elections.
terms.example: Follower A persists the new entry in its local log.

terms.plain: More than half the cluster has durably stored the same entry.
terms.example: At least two of three nodes must acknowledge before commit.

terms.plain: The cluster accepts an entry as stable history that the state machine may apply.
terms.example: The Leader advances commit index after majority replication.

timeline.must: Do not learn Raft in general; learn enough to change replication code tomorrow.
The Leader, not an arbitrary follower, chooses the order of writes.
One follower storing the entry does not make the entry safe.
Commit index moves only after a majority persists the entry.

core.heading: Writes begin at the Leader
core.body: A client does not update every server directly. It sends the request to the Leader, which creates an ordered log entry and fans it out to followers.

core.heading: Replicated is not yet committed
core.body: An entry on one follower exists on one replica only. It has not crossed the majority-confirmation boundary, so it is not yet stable history for the state machine.

core.heading: Majority acknowledgement is the commit condition
core.body: After a majority durably stores the entry, the Leader can advance commit index. Only committed entries may be applied in order by the state machine.

formula: Client → Leader appends → replicate in parallel → majority ack → commit → apply

visuals.caption: The check mark appears only after the entry reaches a majority of replicas.
Follow the arrows: the client contacts the Leader, and the Leader fans out the log entry.

visualThesis: The animation separates replication from commit: log bars mean a replica stored the entry; the check mark means the cluster reached a majority.
visualRead: Count the replicas before deciding whether an entry is committed.
In code, keep ordinary append state separate from commit index.
trap: Do not treat “one follower received the entry” as “the entry is committed”. Before majority acknowledgement, the write is not safe to apply.

recall.q: Why is one follower not enough?
recall.a: A single replica does not represent a majority and may disappear when leadership changes.

recall.q: Which two pieces of state should you inspect in the project code?
recall.a: Where the Leader appends and replicates entries, and when commit index is allowed to advance.

memoryHook: Replication is a condition. Majority acknowledgement is the commit.

transcript.text: The goal is to understand the replication code you need to change tomorrow.
A client sends its write to the Leader, which gives the log entry an order.
The Leader replicates to followers. One local copy is not yet a commit.
After a majority persists the entry, commit index advances and the state machine may apply it.
